title: Zoom! IndyCar Racers Take Over Washington D.C.'s National Mall
summary:
Have you ever seen a race car zoom down a street right in front of famous buildings? This weekend, that's happening in Washington, D.C.! For the first time ever, IndyCar race cars will zip around the National Mall, right by the Capitol building and the Washington Monument. It's called the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, and it's a huge deal because it's a one-time-only event to celebrate America's 250th birthday.

The race is on Sunday, and drivers will go 147 laps around a 1.7-mile track. That's about 250 miles total! The track has seven sharp turns, and the cars can go super fast—up to 190 miles per hour down Pennsylvania Avenue. President Trump even said that's amazing because the road wasn't designed for racing.

This race is part of the IndyCar series, which is like the major league of open-wheel racing in North America. The most famous IndyCar race is the Indianapolis 500, but this one is extra special because it's in the middle of the nation's capital. Some of the best drivers in the world are coming, like Alex Palou and Felix Rosenqvist.

But not everyone is happy. Some art experts worry that the vibrations from the race cars could damage the precious artifacts inside the Smithsonian museums nearby. The race goes right past the Air and Space Museum and the American History Museum.

If you want to watch, general admission tickets were free, but they were given out by lottery and are all gone now. About 288,000 people applied! Organizers expect around 140,000 fans each day. If you can't be there, you can watch it live on Fox. The race starts at 1 p.m. and should take about 2 1/2 hours. So grab some popcorn and get ready for some super-fast fun!
why_it_matters: This story shows how communities try to balance fun celebrations with protecting important history and treasures that belong to everyone.

background_read: Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States, and the National Mall is the long green park at its center where famous monuments and museums sit.
IndyCar is a North American open-wheel car-racing series that has been around for more than 100 years; its most famous race, the Indianapolis 500, began in 1911.
The Smithsonian museums are a group of free U.S. museums that care for historic objects, and car races normally happen on closed tracks, so holding one on public streets beside them is very unusual.
Article_Structure: WHO: IndyCar drivers like Alex Palou and Felix Rosenqvist, plus race organizers, museum experts, and fans.
WHAT: The first-ever Freedom 250 Grand Prix, a one-time-only race with 147 laps on a temporary 1.7-mile track.
WHERE: On the National Mall in Washington, D.C., past the Capitol, the Washington Monument, and the Smithsonian museums.
WHY: To celebrate America's 250th birthday, though some art experts worry that vibrations could damage precious artifacts.

perspectives.description: They see this as a historic, thrilling event that celebrates America's birthday and brings world-class racing to the capital.
They worry that engine vibrations could damage precious artifacts and that public streets near museums are a risky place for a very fast race.
They want to manage huge crowds, road closures, and safety while balancing a big free event with the needs of the city.
